title: Your First Week With a Kitchen Display System
summary: A kitchen display doesn't fix your ticket flow — it shows you that you don't have one, which is exactly what a new operation needs to see.
body_markdown:
A kitchen display system is a screen that replaces paper tickets: orders arrive from your register and your online ordering in one queue, each ticket shows how long it's been waiting, and your cooks clear items as they finish them. If you're just starting out, the reason to care isn't the technology. It's that a new operation's biggest problem is that nobody knows what to make next, and that confusion is what makes service slow and reviews bad.


The screen doesn't fix your flow. It shows you that you don't have one. That's the useful part, and it's why the first week with it matters more than which one you bought.


If you're still deciding whether you need one at all, I wrote[the honest version of that question](https://www.avocadopos.com/blog/do-food-trucks-need-kitchen-display-system) — not every operation does. This post is about what to do once you've got one.


## Why paper tickets fail a new operation specifically


Paper works fine for an experienced crew that's run the same menu for two years. It falls apart in a new operation for reasons that have nothing to do with the paper:


-


**Nobody knows the priority.** Six tickets are up. Which one is oldest? On paper you're reading handwriting and guessing. Tickets get worked in the order somebody grabbed them, which means the person who's been waiting longest waits longer.


-


**Online orders and window orders live in different worlds.** A new operator takes an online order, puts it on a sticky note, and forgets it until the customer walks up. This is the single most common cause of a bad first review.


-


**Nothing tells you you're behind.** You feel busy. You don't know that ticket four has been sitting for eleven minutes until somebody at the window asks about it.


-


**Modifiers get missed.** "No onions" written small, in grease, at speed. Every missed modifier is a remake, and a remake during a rush costs you three other orders.


All four of those are the same problem: the information exists but it isn't visible to the person who needs it at the moment they need it.


## Setting up your ticket flow in week one


Do these in order. Most people skip straight to step four and then wonder why the screen didn't help.


1.


**Decide who touches the screen.** One person. On a truck or a small kitchen, the screen is owned by whoever expedites — the person handing food out the window. If everybody clears tickets, nobody knows what's actually done.


2.


**Write down your target ticket time.** Pick a real number for your menu — the time from order placed to food handed over that you think is achievable at a normal pace. You need this number before the timers mean anything. Without it, a screen full of counters is just anxiety.


3.


**Set your alert thresholds to match.** A ticket's timer should change color or make noise before you're late, not after. If your target is eight minutes, you want to be warned at five.


4.


**Run one full service without changing anything.** Resist tuning mid-rush. You're collecting information about where your flow actually breaks.


5.


**Fix the one thing that broke most.** Usually it's a single menu item that takes three times longer than everything else, or a station that's downstream of a bottleneck. One change per service.


The timers do the work here. In Avocado's KDS every ticket counts up from the moment the order is placed, with audible alerts at the five, ten, and fifteen minute marks and colors that escalate as a ticket ages — so being behind is something you hear, not something a customer tells you. Scheduled and delivery orders count down to their pickup time instead, which is the behavior you want: a 7pm order isn't late at 6:40.


## What actually speeds up service


A screen alone doesn't make food faster. These are the things that do, and the screen is what makes them visible:


Change


Why it works


Work tickets oldest-first, always


Your slowest ticket is what generates complaints, not your average one


Clear items as they're finished, not whole tickets


The expediter can see a ticket is three-quarters done and stage it, instead of finding out at the end


Cut the one item that blocks the line


On a truck, one four-minute item during a rush costs you every order behind it


Put online orders in the same queue as the window


Two queues means one gets forgotten, and it's always the one without a face attached


Pre-stage anything that can be pre-staged


The screen shows you what you're always making, which tells you what to prep


Say the ticket number out loud when you clear it


Free, and it catches the mismatch between what's made and what's handed over


The second row is the one new operators underuse. Clearing individual items instead of whole tickets is what lets one person expedite for a two-person kitchen, because the status of every order is on the screen instead of in someone's head.


And that third row connects to something bigger. A menu item's value isn't just its margin — it's margin against the time it occupies your window. A high-margin item that takes four minutes can earn you less per hour than a cheaper one you hand over in forty seconds. That's[profit per minute of line time](https://www.avocadopos.com/blog/profit-per-minute-of-line-time) , and once you can see ticket times you can finally act on it.


## How this shows up in your reviews


Read bad reviews of new restaurants and trucks. Very few say the food was bad. They say it took forty minutes, or the order was wrong, or an online order wasn't ready at the promised time.


Those are all flow failures, not cooking failures. Which means they're the failures most likely to improve in your first month — and the ones that do the most damage early, because a new operation with six reviews can't absorb a one-star the way an established one can.


Being honest about the ceiling: a display system helps with wait times and order accuracy. It does nothing about a menu that's too big, a line cook who needs training, or a truck with one fryer. If your service is slow because you're under-equipped, the screen will just tell you that very precisely.


The other half of protecting your early reviews is catching the unhappy customer before they get home and open Google. That's a separate system, and it matters as much as speed does — I wrote about[how to catch bad feedback before it becomes a public review](https://www.avocadopos.com/blog/catch-bad-reviews-before-they-happen) .


## The honest caveat


Three things worth knowing before you set this up.


A screen is one more thing that can fail. It needs power and a working connection to your register, and a truck at a festival has neither reliably. Know how you'd take and fulfill orders if the screen went dark mid-rush, and practice it once on a slow day rather than discovering it at a rush.


It also adds a step for very small operations. If you're one person cooking and handing out food, a screen may genuinely be slower than looking at the order on your register. The break-even is roughly when a second person joins, or when online orders start arriving while you're serving a window.


And it doesn't retroactively tell you much. A live timer tells you a ticket is running long right now. That's the job. Don't set it up expecting a report of your average prep time by item over the last month — build the habit of hitting your target time first, and let the numbers come later.


## Where doing this by hand breaks down


You can run flow on paper with a good crew. New operators mostly can't, because the thing that makes paper work is everybody already knowing what happens next.


The wall is the moment you have two order sources at once — someone at the window and an online order due in six minutes — and one pair of hands deciding between them. That decision gets made badly under pressure, every time, unless both orders are in the same queue with a visible clock on each.


Avocado's kitchen display puts window, online, and scheduled orders in one queue with live timers on every ticket, and lets you clear items one at a time instead of whole orders.


*Avocado is a POS built for independent restaurants and food trucks. We're operators first, and we'd rather tell you the honest version than the version that closes faster.*
